To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the functional integral for a gauge theory, if it exists, is gauge invariant and Lorentz invariant, (2) the Lagrangian form of the functional integral for gauge theories, if it exists at all, is neither gauge invariant nor Lorentz invariant (unless the gauge group is abelian and the gauge theory is free of anomalies).

(1) the naive Lagrangians of abelian anomalous theories are not gauge invariant and that (2) a reformulation in terms of gauge invariant covariant anomalies is possible, but that (3) Lorentz in- variance is lost in both formulations.

the functional integral for a 4-dimensional Abelian gauge theory with a chiral fermion is different from the naive Lagranian form, that a reformulation is possible using (gauge-)covariant anomalies, that Lorentz invariace seems to be violated, and that the 2-dimensional chiral Schwinger-model leads to the usual gauge invariant formulation that is Lorentz-invariant.

Lorentz invariants are not always Lorentz invariant.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gauge invariant reformulation of the four-dimensional anomalous theory seems not to be possible.
the functional integral is not a gauge invariant functional of the gauge potential, but of the gauge covariant field strength.
the functional integral for an abelian anomalous theory, if it exists, is gauge and Lorentz noninvariant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the naive Lagrangians of abelian gauge theories are not the most general ones.

the naive functional integral for a gauge theory with a non-trivial gauge anomaly is not a gauge invariant object, and that a covariant gauge invariant reformulation of the theory requires a covariant formulation of the anomalies as well.
the functional integral for an anomalous gauge theory can only be defined by using (gauge-)covariant anomalies.
